content: The third conditional imagines a past
that did not happen — and its result.
if + had done, would have done:
"If you had left earlier, you would
have missed the traffic."
(But you didn't leave early, so you
hit the traffic.)
Both halves are unreal. The if-half
uses had + done; the result-half uses
would have + done.
Many languages build this with one
mood across both halves; English pairs
had done with would have done.
wish + had done looks back with regret
at a past you cannot change.
"I wish I had known." = but I didn't,
and I am sorry now.
if only is the same wish, felt harder:
"If only he had taken the pill."
To undo it now would take a miracle.
The verb steps back to had + done — the
same shape the third conditional uses
in its if-half.
Many languages mark this regret with a
special 'if only' word; English bends
wish onto had + done.
When we report a question, we do not
keep the question word order.
Direct: "Where do you live?"
Reported: She asked me where I lived.
The word order flattens to a statement
(where I LIVED, not where DID I live),
and the tense steps back a step.
For yes/no questions, use whether or if:
"Is the internet down?" becomes
He asked me whether the internet was
down.
To report an order or a request, use
tell/ask someone + to + verb.
Direct: "Turn it off."
Reported: She told me to turn it off.
Direct: "Please wait."
Reported: He asked me to wait.
For a negative order, put not before to:
"Don't touch it." becomes
They told me not to touch it.
Many languages report speech word for
word inside quotation marks; English
re-shapes it — order flattens, tenses
step back, commands turn to 'to do'.
